newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 3.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Sept 3.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH

-- BUNZL AHEAD AS PRESSURES EASE The paper and packaging group, Bunzl, yesterday reported a 12 per cent rise interim pre-tax profits to 55.8 million pounds stg and said the deflationary pressures that constrained its first half sales growth are easing.

-- BUYERS IN WINGS FOR NEWSPAPER Sunday Business, which was put into voluntary administration in June, could be sold by the end of the week, according to the newspaper's administrators Royce Peeling Green, who say two serious bids have been attracted. They added that the newspaper's creditors would be told on September 17 what they can expect to recover from the proceeds of the sale.

-- SUPER JUMBO HITS TURBULENCE Boeing clashed yesterday with its European rival Airbus Industrie in the race to develop the superjumbo. Boeing disputed Airbus claims about the size of the market for planes carrying 500 or more passengers as well as the cost of developing them. Boeing estimated that demand was unlikely to top 470 and it estimated the cost of developing the new aircraft at between $12 and $15 billion, compared to the $8 billion that Airbus intends to invest, while estimating that demand would reach 1,400 over 20 years.
THE TIMES

-- RISING FACTORY OUTPUT STIFLES RATE CUT HOPES After a long period of stagnation, British manufacturing expanded at its fastest rate since spring last year in August according to the latest report from the Chartered Institute of Purchasing and Supply. It is now less likely that the Chancellor will risk an all out fight with the Bank of England by cutting base rates tomorrow.

-- MORGAN GRENFELL FUNDS SUSPENDED After discovering possible irregularities in the valuation of the fund's shareholdings, Morgan Grenfell's investment management arm has suspended dealings in funds worth 1.4 billion pounds stg. Investigations centre on the European Growth Fund, as well as two smaller funds, Europa and European Capital Growth. Morgan Grenfell and the Investment Management Organisation, the regulator, were unable to say how long the suspensions would last.
-- AEA SELL-OFF VALUE LIKELY TO BE SET AT 200 MILLION POUNDS

The privatisation of AEA Technology, which provides decommissioning and waste management services to the nuclear power industry got under way yesterday, with the publication of the pathfinder prospectus. This is the Government's last privatisation before the general election. The expected value of AEA is around 200 million pounds stg. Only 10 per cent of the shares available are for private sale, with 80 per cent to be placed with institutional investors, with 10 per cent reserved for the company's 3,500 employees.
THE GUARDIAN

-- GEC BACKS AWAY FROM PAY ROW. GEC yesterday agreed to revise the remuneration package on offer to its new managing director George Simpson. In a statement issued last night, GEC said Mr Simpson's long term incentive scheme had been altered, with his bonus only being awarded if GEC's share price remains 10 per cent higher than the growth in the FTSE 100 share index for three years, rather than six months as in the original contract.

-- HOUSE PRICES RISE 'FASTEST SINCE 1989' House prices are rising faster than at any time since October 1989 according to the Halifax building society, with annual price growth in August up to 5.7 per cent. The relatively small monthly increase of 0.5 per cent in August is seen as proof that the upturn will be sustained.
-- CASH-RICH ALLDERS RETURNS 50 MILLION POUNDS TO INVESTORS IN SPECIAL DIVIDEND

The Allders department store group is to return 50 million pounds stg to shareholders through a special dividend, after selling its duty-free business earlier this year. The group is also to reduce its share capital by exchanging 15 new shares for every 19 existing shares, thus reducing the group's shares by 21 per cent to 85.1 million, but their value will be higher.
THE INDEPENDENT

-- UNILEVER PLANNING 7 BILLION CAMPAIGN TO CATCH ARCH-RIVALS Unilever, the Anglo-Dutch consumer goods company has plans to sell or close down businesses accounting for up to 7 billion pounds stg in sales in an attempt to put it back into contention with rival Procter & Gamble. The company is to concentrate on streamlining a brands portfolio that is about 1,000 strong.

-- UNISON TO SUE OVER PENSION MIS-SELLING Unison, Britain's biggest union, is to join the legal battle against large life companies and financial advisers for allegedly mis-selling personal pension plans. Unison, the public service union will join the GMB general union and teachers' unions in suing companies for selling policies under which individuals claim to have lost thousands of pounds in benefits.

-- SINGER & FRIEDLANDER PROFITS SURGE 41 PER CENT Singer & Friedlander yesterday reported a 41 per cent surge in half-year profits to 21 million pounds stg before exceptional items. The profits growth was driven by investment management and the contribution from its new stockbroking activities. The bank vowed to remain one of Britain's last remaining independent merchant banks.
